newsitem.title: USA: NABE sees no major inflation risk, small rate hike.
newsitem.headline: NABE sees no major inflation risk, small rate hike.

text.p: In a somewhat surprising but encouraging take on inflation, only about one third of the experts of the National Association of Business Economists (NABE) predicted a small monetary policy tightening in the next six months.
And three out of four NABE experts called U.S. monetary policy too restrictive since the January easing.

"Thirty-nine percent (of the panelists) expects policy to become more restrictive over the next six months," the NABE said on Monday while releasing its 41-member panel's outlook at its annual conference in Boston.

"The median expected (5.25-percent federal funds) interest rate increase is only 25-50 basis points," the NABE, which represents a broad cross-section of U.S. forecasters, added. "Less than one-quarter of the NABE panel is looking for a rate hike before December 1996. About 27 percent expect a Fed tightening by March 1997."
The NABE also agreed with a view expressed by a majority at the Fed that monetary policy is somewhat restrictive.
"Seventy-eight percent of the NABE panel thinks that monetary policy has been too restrictive over the past six months," the NABE said.
For 1996-97, the NABE saw the U.S. Consumer Price Index averaging 3.0 percent versus a May forecast of 2.9 percent.

"Only 10 percent of the NABE panel thinks inflation is 'truly dead', with 81 percent saying it is "only temporarily subdued," the NABE said, noting only "five percent of the NABE panel now feels that inflation is the most serious problem facing the economy today, up from only two percent in May."
The NABE outlook also shows that only two percent of the panel members cited recession as a major concern -- the same percentage as for crime and consumer debt.
In a vote of confidence for the Federal Reserve, the NABE ranked monetary policy last among the threats to the U.S. economy and agreed with the Fed's own, often-stated goal.

"Seventy-two percent thinks the best way for the Fed to foster long-term growth is to focus on price stability," the NABE said, while giving a definition of price stability much in line with a range recently cited by Federal Reserve Bank of New York President William McDonough.
Sixty-five percent of the panel thinks CPI annualized increases between 1.0 percent and less than 2.0 percent would equate price stability, the NABE found.
The NABE saw Gross Domestic Product growth averaging 2.3 percent in 1996-97 versus a 2.2-percent forecast in May.

Such a forecast is consistent with non-inflationary growth as "the long-term growth potential of the U.S. economy is above 2.5 percent according to 49 percent of the NABE policy panel and in the 2.0-2.5-percent range according to another 48 percent."
The NABE tied their 2.5-percent growth potential estimate to the notion productivity gains in the services-heavy U.S. economy may be understated.
"Fully 69 percent of the NABE policy panel thinks that productivity gains in the service sector are undertstated," the NABE reported.

In line with expectations of modest Fed moves, the NABE forecast only moderate fluctuations in market rates with the three-month Tresury bill averaging "5.1 in September, and 5.2 percent in December 1996 and March 1997 and June 1997."
The NABE also expected the 30-year Treasury bond yield "to average 6.9 percent in September and December 1996 and inch down to 6.8 percent in March and June 1997."
Turning to the stock market, the NABE saw a 9.5-percent profit gain in 1996, "less than double-digit gains" earlier.
"Nonetheless, two-thirds of the NABE forecast panel didn't worry a continuation of a stock market decline would lead to recession," the NABE concluded.

Among the threats to the U.S. economy, the NABE ranked growth in government spendings/entitlements as the top single concern (17 percent), followed by low productivity/slow growth in living standard (14 percent), poor training/education (11 percent), the federal deficit and income inequality (nine percent), and low savings and job security (eight percent).
